notes:
I worked through Matthew 14 using enduringword.com (Guzik), Ellicott (on biblehub and studylight), preceptaustin.org (which collects Lenski, Hiebert, MacArthur, Barton and others), Matthew Henry (on blueletterbible), Calvin (on studylight), Spurgeon (on preceptaustin) and a few shorter pages.

**Gaps you should know about first:**
- **Protestant traditions:** I didn't find pages where one tradition's teachers argue against another's on this chapter. The real disagreements I found are between individual commentators, mainly over Peter in vv. 28–31 and over touching Jesus' cloak in vv. 34–36. The pages don't say which tradition these writers belong to, so I haven't labelled them.
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I found only one catholic.com article on v. 27, plus an early sermon quoted on biblehub. Nothing from newadvent.org or oca.org.
- **Prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace:** Nothing found on any of these.
- **Modern scholarship:** The only scholarly notes I found came quoted inside other pages, not from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org themselves.

---

**v. 1**
- This Herod is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. "Tetrarch" literally means "the ruler of a fourth part," but came to be used of any subordinate ruler. A tetrarch was lower than a king; Antipas later asked Caligula for the title of king and was refused. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/
- Ellicott suggests who may have told Herod about Jesus: the nobleman of Capernaum, Manaen (raised with the tetrarch), or Chuza his steward. He adds that the word for "servants" is not the word for slaves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Matthew Henry: just when Jesus' own townspeople looked down on him, he became famous at court. God honours those who are despised for his sake. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: Herod's guilt and superstition led him to this fear. He passes on Barclay's report that Origen said Jesus and John looked very alike. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/
- Ellicott: Herod sided with the Sadducees, who denied resurrection, yet the superstitious terror of a guilty conscience was stronger than his Sadducee scepticism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Spurgeon: he had enough conscience to scare him, but not enough to change him. If Herod credited a risen man with such power, Spurgeon asks, shouldn't we believe in the power of our risen Lord? https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary-spurgeon
- Preceptaustin: Herod knew John did no miracles in life, so his muddled theology decided the powers must come from a resurrection. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary
- Calvin: people admit Jesus has divine power, yet turn him into other men in their imaginations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-14.html

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: Josephus names Machaerus in Perea as the place where the Baptist was imprisoned and killed. Herodias was niece to both of her husbands. Ellicott calls the marriage adulterous and, under the law of Moses, doubly incestuous. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- MacArthur (quoted on preceptaustin): Antipas seduced Herodias away from his half-brother Philip while visiting Rome, and divorced his wife, the daughter of King Aretas, to marry her. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary
- Matthew Henry: Herod jailed John partly out of his own revenge and partly to please Herodias, who seems the more furious of the two. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm

**v. 4**
- Guzik, citing France: Herod imprisoned John for boldly rebuking the king's sin. The verb "said" is in the imperfect tense, which may mean John kept saying it, like an ongoing campaign. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/
- Poole: John saw Herod living in adultery and incest, and told him plainly that God's law forbade such a marriage. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/matthew-14.html
- Ellicott: Josephus gives a broader reason, that Antipas feared John's preaching might stir up a popular revolt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: like many today, Herod feared people's opinion before he feared God. Fear of man was the only thing holding him back from worse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/
- Ellicott: Mark adds that Herod himself feared John as a just and holy man. Conscience fought against passion in Herod, as in Ahab facing Elijah. Herodias, like Jezebel, never wavered. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: some critics think the "birthday" was really the anniversary of Herod's accession, but Ellicott sees no reason not to take it literally. For a royal daughter to dance before the banqueters was something any decent Jew would shudder at. Josephus names her Salome. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Guzik, citing France: the Greek word for "girl" can describe someone of marriageable age, so she was at least a teenager. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/
- Spurgeon applies it to modern mothers and immodest dancing, warning that in this case dancing led to a cruel crime. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: stories of lavish rewards to dancers circulated at the time, and Herod may have been copying Rome's imperial court. He probably imagined she would ask for a jewel, a bracelet, a palace or a city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: an oath must be lawfully taken and lawfully kept, and Herod broke both rules. He swore an oath about something vain and foolish, with no need to. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/matthew-14.html

**v. 8** (commentators disagree on how long this was planned)
- Ellicott: "prompted" does not mean she was coached before the dance. Mark says she left the hall afterwards to ask her mother what to request. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Guzik takes the opposite view: the request shows that Herodias had planned this for some time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/
- Matthew Henry goes further and suspects that Herod himself was in on the plot, and his talk of his oath and his guests was a sham. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm
- Lenski: the girl never hesitated, despite the crime and the gruesomeness of the gift. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: this was conscience's last struggle. Like most weak men, Herod feared being thought weak. A false concern for what people would say pushed him into guilt instead of holding him back. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Spurgeon: rash promises and oaths are no excuse for doing wrong. The promise was void, because no one has the right to promise to do wrong. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary-spurgeon
- Matthew Henry: it is a great mistake to think a wicked oath justifies a wicked act. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: the plural "oaths" suggests Herod had repeated his oath. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/matthew-14.html

**v. 10**
- Preceptaustin: Herod was not a true king, but he did have authority to carry out the death penalty. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary
- Ellicott pauses to reflect on John's greatness, and notes that the Forerunner's conviction, that repentance must be preached before forgiveness, has reappeared in every great revival. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm

**v. 11**
- Ellicott on what happened afterwards: Herod and Herodias were later deposed and banished to Lyons in Gaul. A legend says Salome died retributively, her head cut off in a fall on ice, but Josephus records only her two marriages. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Guzik's account of their end: in Gaul, Herod and Herodias committed suicide. This differs from Ellicott, who says only that they died there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: from this point John's followers probably stopped being a separate community in Judea, though Apollos and the disciples at Ephesus show they survived elsewhere (Acts 18–19). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Spurgeon (via Guzik): the text says they buried "the body", not John, because the real John no man could bury. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/

**v. 13**
- Guzik: Jesus' withdrawal was not cowardice, but an understanding of the Father's timing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/
- Ellicott suggests two motives: personal grief at John's death, and a wish not to become the centre of the public excitement it caused. The Twelve had also just returned, and Passover pilgrims crowded the roads. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Matthew Henry: when God opens a way of escape in danger, it is lawful to flee, unless God specially calls us to stay. He also notes that more people seem to have crowded to Christ after John's martyrdom than before. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm

**v. 14**
- Calvin: Jesus saw starving souls. As Mark puts it, they were like sheep without a shepherd, and though worn out, Jesus did not spare himself. Calvin also notes that Matthew mentions only miracles, but we can conclude Jesus did not leave out teaching. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-14.html
- Spurgeon: Jesus was not angry or disappointed at losing his quiet; he was moved with compassion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 15**
- Spurgeon: the disciples' request really meant "Get us out of the difficulty." https://www.preceptaustin.org/c-h-spurgeon-exposition-of-matthew
- Matthew Henry: Christ's disciples are often more careful to show good sense than zeal. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm
- Ellicott: this is the only miracle recorded by all four Gospels, and an act of creative power. He calls the rationalist explanation, that Jesus' example shamed people into sharing hidden food, ridiculously inadequate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm

**v. 16**
- Guzik: Jesus tested both the disciples' compassion and their faith, but did not ask them to meet the need without guiding them through it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/
- D. A. Carson (quoted on preceptaustin): if they had remembered the wine at Cana, they would have asked Jesus to meet the need, not send the people away. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary
- Matthew Henry: those who have Christ have enough, and need not go elsewhere for happiness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm

**v. 17**
- Guzik: the food came from a boy (John 6:9). It is to the disciples' credit that they travelled light and trusted Jesus to provide. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/

**v. 18**
- Spurgeon: Jesus wants us to hand over all we have without holding back. He will accept it and make a little go a long way. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 19**
- Guzik: sitting on the grass suggests a banquet-like atmosphere of enjoyment. Jesus may have used the familiar Jewish mealtime blessing. He chose to work through the disciples' hands, though he didn't need to. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/
- Ellicott: in John 6 the miracle becomes the starting point for the teaching about eating the flesh of the true Bread from heaven, a figure of communion with Christ's life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm

**v. 20**
- Ellicott: the basket here is a cophinus, a small hand basket that travellers often used to carry food. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Guzik: God did not want the leftovers wasted. He also sees the meal as a preview of the great messianic banquet. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/

**v. 21** (estimates of the crowd's size differ)
- Guzik: perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 people in total. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/
- Ellicott: Matthew alone mentions women and children. They were probably few, grouped separately and not counted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Utley (bible.org): perhaps six or seven thousand in all, though this is uncertain. https://bible.org/seriespage/matthew-14
- A NET Bible note (quoted on preceptaustin) records that many commentators think the feedings of the 5,000 and the 4,000 were one event, but points to differences between them, such as the numbers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary

**v. 22**
- Barclay (on studylight) explains why Jesus "made" the disciples leave: John tells us the crowd wanted to make him king by force. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/14-29.html
- Spurgeon: Jesus always takes the heavier task. Only he who seated them for the feast could send them home. https://www.preceptaustin.org/c-h-spurgeon-exposition-of-matthew

**v. 23**
- Ellicott: Jesus may have sensed in the crowd's enthusiasm something like a renewal of the wilderness temptation, needing special communion with his Father. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Matthew Henry: Christ here set an example of secret prayer, praying as a man in the form of a servant. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm

**v. 24**
- Matthew Henry: the disciples kept heading where they had been sent. Troubles may disturb us in our duty, but must not drive us from it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm
- Spurgeon sees the boat as the church today, tossed by contrary winds, but while Christ pleads for it, it can never sink. https://www.preceptaustin.org/c-h-spurgeon-exposition-of-matthew

**v. 25**
- Gill (on biblehub): the fourth watch was about three hours before sunrise. The Jews had adopted the Roman division of the night into four three-hour watches. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/14-27.htm
- Ligonier: ancient Jews saw the sea as a terrifying enemy that only God could tame (Job 38:8–11). https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/walking-on-the-sea-of-galilee
- Sam Storms: in walking on the water, Jesus is doing what only God can do. He links this to Job 9:8. https://www.samstorms.org/enjoying-god-blog/post/-he-meant-to-pass-by-them-
- Barclay (on studylight) holds that the Greek allows two interpretations, one of which is that Jesus actually walked on the water. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/14-29.html

**v. 26**
- An older commentary quoted on biblehub: belief in spirits was not strange in that age, though the Sadducees denied it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/14-27.htm
- GotQuestions: the disciples didn't recognise Jesus in the storm, and sometimes we don't recognise him in ours. https://www.gotquestions.org/Peter-walking-on-water.html

**v. 27** (Protestants and Catholics broadly agree here)
- Ligonier: "It is I" translates ego eimi, the Greek form of God's covenant name "I am", a strong hint of Jesus' deity. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/walking-on-the-sea-of-galilee
- Sam Storms reads it as "I am the I am!": in Jesus we meet the God of Israel in human flesh. https://www.samstorms.org/enjoying-god-blog/post/-he-meant-to-pass-by-them-
- Catholic (catholic.com) admits that ego eimi can simply be a way of identifying oneself. But because it comes with power over wind and sea, which belongs to God in the Old Testament, it echoes the burning bush. Jesus was telling them, "I'm God!" https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-divinity-of-jesus-according-to-mark
- Ellicott: in later years the moment took on a symbolic meaning for the disciples and the wider church, as Christ coming through the storms of persecution. https://biblehub.com/matthew/14-27.htm

**v. 28** (commentators genuinely differ over Peter)
- Lenski defends Peter: Jesus accepted Peter's faith, and would never have said "Come" if the faith were false. Critics of Peter are really criticising Jesus. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary
- Barton: Peter was not testing Jesus; he was the only one in the boat who responded in faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary
- Spurgeon is more mixed: genuine faith, mixed with the imperfection and presumption so typical of Peter. https://www.preceptaustin.org/c-h-spurgeon-exposition-of-matthew
- Matthew Henry: when the Pharisees asked for a sign, Jesus rebuked them. When Peter asked, he got it, because he asked intending to trust Christ. But we should not expect extraordinary commands like Peter's today; we have the general rules of Scripture. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm
- Guzik: Peter's "if" is a real condition, almost "since it's you." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/

**v. 29**
- Gill: Christ walked on water by his own power as God; Peter was held up by Christ's power. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/14-29.html
- Clarke warns against testing Christ's power out of curiosity, or even to strengthen faith when ordinary means are available. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/14-29.html
- Matthew Henry: Peter walked on the water not for show, but to go to Jesus. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm

**v. 30**
- Matthew Henry: Christ called Peter so he would learn Christ's power by walking and his own weakness by sinking. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm
- Preceptaustin (a sermon outline): Peter was wise to cry out as soon as he began to sink. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary

**v. 31**
- Guzik: Jesus' question shows that doubt is a divided mind, not a single-minded focus on Jesus. Even little faith is real faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/
- Lenski: the question can never be answered, because there is no sensible answer. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary
- Bailey (quoted on preceptaustin): doubt is evidence of a divided mind. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary

**v. 32**
- Ellicott: mountain squalls usually died down slowly, but here the wind stopped at once, as their Lord entered the boat. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Matthew Henry: Christ got into the boat instead of walking to shore, because when ordinary means are available, miracles are not to be expected. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm

**v. 33**
- Guzik: this was the disciples' first plainly open acknowledgement of his divine identity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-14/
- Preceptaustin notes the contrast with Mark, who says the disciples were amazed and their hearts were hardened because they hadn't understood the loaves. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-14-commentary
- An early sermon quoted on biblehub reads the whole scene as an allegory: the sea is the present world, and Peter is a type of the one Church. https://biblehub.com/study/matthew/14-27.htm

**vv. 34–36** (Calvin and Ellicott read the touching differently)
- Calvin: nothing here supports seeking God's grace in wood, nails or robes. In his view, God put up with the people's weakness for a time. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-14.html
- Ellicott: the belief came from the earlier healing in Matthew 9:20–22, and the touch implied faith, the condition for receiving, so it worked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/14.htm
- Matthew Henry spiritualises it: when we mix faith with the word and submit to it, we touch the hem of Christ's garment. He also says Christ is trusted as far as he is known. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_014.cfm
- The ICC (a modern critical commentary) argues that in Matthew the sequence is distorted: Matthew dropped Mark's account of the apostles' mission, so he introduces Herod with a vague "at that time." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/icc/matthew-14.html
